grammar_topic: used to, be used to, get used to
title: Getting Used to a New Country
body: When I first moved abroad, I used to feel completely lost every time I left my apartment, unable to read basic signs or understand simple conversations. I wasn't used to the silence of small talk disappearing entirely, replaced by an awkward, constant translation happening inside my head. Slowly, though, I've been getting used to ordering food by pointing rather than speaking, and nobody seems to mind anymore. I used to panic in supermarkets, overwhelmed by unfamiliar packaging, though now I'm used to recognising at least the basics. My neighbour, who moved here decades ago, says she's completely used to it now, though she still remembers how disorienting those first months felt. 'You never fully get used to everything,' she admitted honestly, 'but eventually the strange becomes ordinary without you quite noticing when it happened.' I used to call home every single day, desperate for something familiar, though now I'm used to a comfortable weekly call instead. My colleagues have gotten used to my occasional grammar mistakes, and I've gotten used to laughing about them myself. Looking back at who I used to be during those first confusing weeks, I barely recognise that anxious, exhausted version of myself, now so thoroughly used to a life I once found impossibly foreign.

words.context: How disorienting those first months felt.
A life I once found impossibly foreign.
That anxious, exhausted version of myself.

grammar_topic: gerunds and infinitives (advanced patterns, including verb + object + infinitive)
title: Would You Mind Helping Me?
body: My new colleague asked me to help her understand the filing system, something everyone else had simply learned to accept without question. I remember struggling with it myself, years ago, before eventually managing to organise it properly. 'Would you mind explaining it again?' she asked politely, clearly embarrassed to admit she was still confused. I don't mind repeating things, I told her honestly, remembering how kind someone had been to me during my own first confusing weeks. I persuaded her to try a simpler method instead, one I'd developed after giving up on the official system entirely. She stopped taking notes for a moment, just to actually listen properly, and I could see the relief on her face. 'Remember to save a backup copy,' I reminded her, recalling the time I forgot to do exactly that and lost everything. She promised to remember, and I believed her completely. Later, I overheard her helping someone else with the exact same system, patiently explaining it the way I had taught her. I stopped to listen for a moment, quietly proud, remembering my own awkward first days here. Sometimes, I've realised, teaching someone something properly means eventually watching them teach it to someone else entirely.

I persuaded her to try a simpler method.

grammar_topic: past modals of deduction and preference: must have..., would rather
title: The Missing Signature
body: The contract must have been signed sometime last week, though nobody in the office could say exactly when. The manager, clearly frustrated, insisted that someone must have removed the signed copy from the filing cabinet deliberately. 'It can't have simply disappeared,' she said, searching through the same drawer for the third time. Her assistant suggested that perhaps the document had never actually been signed at all, though the manager was certain she remembered watching the client sign it personally. 'I'd rather we didn't accuse anyone without proof,' the assistant said carefully, aware of how tense the office had become. Someone must have moved it accidentally, another colleague offered, perhaps while tidying the shared desk over the weekend. The manager admitted she would rather have checked immediately after the signing, instead of assuming the document was safely filed. Eventually, after nearly an hour of searching, they found it — mistakenly filed under an entirely different client's name. 'I should have double-checked the filing myself,' the assistant admitted quietly. The manager, relieved but still slightly annoyed, said she would rather they created a clearer system than continue relying on memory alone. Nobody had done anything malicious, they eventually agreed; the document simply must have been misplaced during a busy, distracted afternoon.

words.context: I'd rather we didn't accuse anyone.
How tense the office had become.
The document must have been misplaced.
The manager, relieved but still slightly annoyed.
Removed the signed copy from the filing cabinet.

title: Something Tastes Different
body: The soup tasted different tonight, though I couldn't immediately explain why. It smelled richer than usual, as if the chef had added something new to the recipe. My grandmother, tasting it carefully, agreed something felt slightly off, though she couldn't quite identify the missing ingredient either. 'It tastes as though someone forgot the cumin,' she suggested eventually, sounding fairly confident despite her uncertainty. The bread, at least, smelled exactly like always, warm and familiar, though it looked slightly darker than the usual golden colour. My uncle, ever dramatic, declared the whole meal tasted as if it had been prepared by someone entirely different, though he ate two full portions regardless. The kitchen sounded busier than usual too, pots clattering more loudly, voices sounding stressed rather than relaxed. Eventually, the chef admitted she'd tried a completely new recipe, nervous about how everyone would react to the change. 'It sounds like everyone's confused,' she laughed, slightly embarrassed by the unexpected reactions. Once we knew the truth, the soup somehow tasted better, familiar disappointment replaced by curious appreciation. Sometimes, my grandmother said wisely, food tastes different not because something's actually wrong, but simply because change always feels unfamiliar before it feels good.

words.context: Voices sounding stressed rather than relaxed.
Change always feels unfamiliar before it feels good.

grammar_topic: the passive (all forms); have/get something done; it is said that...
title: The House on the Hill
body: It is said that the old house on the hill was built by a wealthy merchant who was never actually seen in town again after it was completed. The windows are believed to have been imported from a distant country, an unusual luxury for such a small town at the time. Every few years, the roof gets repaired by the same local family, though the strange rumours surrounding the house have never been properly explained. It is thought that a fire destroyed part of the original structure decades ago, though records from that period were reportedly lost. Local children are told that the garden was designed by someone who is said to have disappeared mysteriously, though nobody can confirm where this story originated. Last year, the gate was finally fixed, having been broken for as long as most residents can remember. It's rumoured that the house will eventually be sold, though the same rumour has apparently been repeated for at least a decade. The current owner, an elderly woman, has had the interior completely renovated, though she refuses to discuss why the house was neglected for so long beforehand. Whatever actually happened generations ago, the house is still spoken of quietly, as though revealing too much might somehow disturb whatever secret it's believed to be hiding.

words.context: An unusual luxury for such a small town.
The strange rumours surrounding the house.
A fire destroyed part of the structure.
As long as most residents can remember.
Why the house was neglected for so long.

title: Who Said What in the Meeting
body: During the meeting, the marketing director suggested delaying the product launch, though the sales team strongly disagreed. He admitted underestimating how long the testing phase would take, which surprised several colleagues who'd raised the same concern weeks earlier. The finance manager warned everyone not to make promises the company couldn't realistically keep, her tone noticeably sharper than usual. Someone insisted that the original deadline remained achievable, refusing to accept any further delay. The director denied ignoring earlier warnings, though his own notes from previous meetings suggested otherwise. His assistant advised him to acknowledge the mistake openly rather than continuing to deny it defensively. Eventually, he admitted making an error in the original timeline, a rare and noticeably uncomfortable moment for someone usually so confident. The sales lead suggested compromising on a slightly later date, one that satisfied both urgency and realistic testing needs. Everyone reluctantly agreed to the new deadline, though the finance manager warned that no further delays would be tolerated. Afterwards, colleagues admitted privately that they respected him more for finally acknowledging the mistake than they would have if he'd continued denying it. Sometimes, someone remarked quietly on the way out, admitting fault turns out to be far more persuasive than any confident denial.

words.context: He admitted underestimating how long it would take.
Suggested compromising on a slightly later date.
No further delays would be tolerated.
Far more persuasive than any confident denial.

title: Despite Everything, the Shop Survived
body: Despite losing half its regular customers during the renovation next door, the little bookshop somehow managed to survive its most difficult year. Although the owner had considered closing permanently, she decided instead to reorganise the whole business in order to attract a different kind of customer. In spite of having almost no marketing budget, she started a small reading club, purely so that regular customers would have a reason to return weekly. Even though online retailers offered lower prices, many locals continued choosing the shop, largely because they valued the personal recommendations she gave so generously. Despite working exhausting hours alone, she refused to hire extra help, worried about the added financial risk. Although profits remained modest throughout the year, she managed to keep every single employee, even during the quietest winter months. In order to survive the coming year, she's now planning a small café corner, so that customers might linger longer over coffee and conversation. Even though the future remains genuinely uncertain, she says she's never regretted the decision to keep going, despite everyone advising her otherwise at the time. In spite of every obstacle, she often tells new customers, a shop like this survives mainly because people, however busy, still occasionally need somewhere quiet to simply browse.

words.context: She decided to reorganise the whole business.

title: So Much Stuff, So Little Space
body: When we started packing for the move, I underestimated how much furniture we'd actually accumulated over the years. The information about the new flat's dimensions had seemed clear enough, but our belongings clearly disagreed. My scissors, my glasses, even my favourite trousers all vanished mysteriously into unlabelled boxes, impossible to find when actually needed. We needed advice from someone experienced, so we called my aunt, who's moved houses more times than anyone else in the family. 'You'll need far less furniture than you think,' she advised confidently, though our growing pile of boxes suggested otherwise. The news that the removal van would arrive a day early caused genuine panic throughout the household. Our luggage alone filled an entire room, quite apart from the furniture still waiting to be wrapped and labelled properly. I found a piece of useful advice online: label boxes by room, not by category, something we'd completely ignored until that point. By the final evening, exhausted and surrounded by scattered clothes, I realised our furniture, however much we owned, mattered far less than simply getting some proper sleep before the actual move began.

words.context: The removal van would arrive a day early.

title: Every Family Brings Something
body: Every autumn, our village holds a harvest festival that all the families genuinely look forward to. Both bakeries in the village compete, good-naturedly, to bake the most impressive bread for the occasion. Every household is expected to contribute something, whether homemade food, handmade decorations, or simply their time helping set up the tables. All of the children participate in a small competition, judged by both the mayor and the oldest resident in the village, a tradition nobody quite remembers starting. Every year, without exception, someone forgets to bring chairs, and every year, without complaint, someone else's family generously shares theirs. Both my grandmothers used to compete fiercely over whose plov tasted better, a rivalry that, delightfully, continues even now between their grandchildren. None of us can quite remember when the festival actually began, though everyone agrees it's existed for as long as the village itself. Every generation adds something small — a new dish, a new game, a slightly updated tradition — while somehow keeping the whole event recognisably the same. This year, both of my daughters are old enough to help properly for the first time, carrying dishes between tables with careful, serious concentration. Every family, in its own particular way, genuinely looks forward to this one predictable, comforting day each year.

words.context: Our village holds a harvest festival.
Every household is expected to contribute something.
A rivalry that continues even now.

title: The Discovery at the Museum
body: The internet exploded with excitement last month after archaeologists announced the discovery of what may be the oldest tool ever found in the region. The government quickly allocated funding for further excavation, recognising the historical importance of the find. Scientists travel to the site twice a year, carefully documenting each new layer uncovered. The tool, made from a material rarely used elsewhere in ancient history, has puzzled researchers since its discovery. At the museum downtown, the exhibit attracts visitors from across the country, many travelling by train specifically for this single display. The curator explained that most people have breakfast, lunch, and even dinner nearby just to spend the whole day exploring the collection. 'This is the most significant discovery this museum has ever hosted,' she said proudly during the opening ceremony. Interestingly, the internet has also spread several inaccurate theories about the tool's origin, something historians now spend considerable time correcting. The government has promised additional resources for research, twice the current annual budget, recognising the site's growing importance. For now, the tool sits carefully protected behind glass, a small object that has, in a few short months, reshaped an entire region's understanding of its own distant past.

words.context: Has puzzled researchers since its discovery.
Has reshaped an entire region's understanding.
